questions.stem: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the law of
questions.explanation: The first law says a body will not change its state of rest or uniform motion unless a resultant force acts. That reluctance to change is called inertia, so the first law is the law of inertia.

distractorRationale.b: The law of gravitation is a separate law of Newton's about the attraction between masses
distractorRationale.c: Conservation of energy is a distinct principle and is not one of Newton's laws
distractorRationale.d: Action and reaction is the third law, not the first

questions.stem: The SI unit of linear momentum is
questions.explanation: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, so its unit is $\text{kg} \times \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1} = \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. This is identical to the newton second, which is why impulse and momentum can be equated.

distractorRationale.a: N m is the joule, the unit of work or energy
distractorRationale.c: This is the newton, the unit of force — it uses acceleration rather than velocity
distractorRationale.d: This is the joule again, written in base units

questions.stem: Calculate the resultant force needed to give a body of mass 1500 kg an acceleration of 2.0 m/s². Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: From Newton's second law, $F = ma = 1500 \times 2.0 = 3000\ \text{N}$. Because mass is in kilograms and acceleration in m/s², the force comes out directly in newtons with no conversion needed.

questions.stem: The mass of a body is a measure of its inertia.
questions.explanation: True. The larger the mass, the greater the force needed to produce a given acceleration, since $a = \frac{F}{m}$. A loaded lorry resists changes in its motion far more than a bicycle does, which is exactly what we mean by having more inertia.

questions.stem: A sprinter of mass 60 kg runs at a steady speed of 8.0 m/s. Calculate his momentum. Give your answer in kilogram metres per second.
questions.explanation: Momentum $p = mv = 60 \times 8.0 = 480\ \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Momentum needs velocity, not acceleration, so no extra division by time is involved.

questions.stem: A body of mass 5.0 kg is acted upon by two forces: 30 N to the right and 10 N to the left. Its acceleration is
questions.explanation: Find the resultant force first: $30 - 10 = 20\ \text{N}$ to the right. Then $a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{20}{5.0} = 4.0\ \text{m/s}^2$ to the right, in the direction of the resultant.

distractorRationale.a: Divided 10 N by 5.0 kg, using only the smaller force
distractorRationale.c: Divided 30 N by 5.0 kg, ignoring the opposing force altogether
distractorRationale.d: Added the two forces (40 N) instead of subtracting them

questions.stem: A trolley of mass 3.0 kg moving at 4.0 m/s collides with a stationary trolley of mass 1.0 kg and the two move off together. Their common velocity is
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved: $m_1u_1 + m_2u_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v$, so $(3.0)(4.0) + 0 = (4.0)v$, giving $v = \frac{12}{4.0} = 3.0\ \text{m/s}$. The combined trolleys move slower than the first trolley because the same momentum is now shared by more mass.

distractorRationale.a: Divided by the wrong mass, using 12 ÷ 12 or the mass of the stationary trolley alone
distractorRationale.c: Assumed the velocity is unchanged, which would violate conservation of momentum
distractorRationale.d: Quoted the total momentum in kg m/s rather than dividing by the total mass

questions.stem: A constant force of 6.0 N acts on a trolley of mass 2.0 kg, initially at rest, for 4.0 s on a frictionless surface. Calculate the final velocity of the trolley. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: First find the acceleration: $a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{6.0}{2.0} = 3.0\ \text{m/s}^2$. Then $v = u + at = 0 + (3.0)(4.0) = 12\ \text{m/s}$. You could also use impulse: $Ft = mv$, so $v = \frac{6.0 \times 4.0}{2.0} = 12\ \text{m/s}$.

options.text: the exhaust gases push against the air below the rocket
the rocket pushes the exhaust gases downwards and the gases push the rocket upwards
the burning fuel makes the rocket lighter than air
gravity is absent at the launch pad

questions.explanation: This is Newton's third law. The rocket exerts a downward force on the escaping gases and the gases exert an equal upward force on the rocket. Because the two forces act on different bodies, they do not cancel, and the rocket accelerates upwards once this thrust exceeds its weight.

distractorRationale.a: No air is needed — rockets work in the vacuum of space, which proves the thrust comes from the gases, not the atmosphere
distractorRationale.c: A rocket is far denser than air throughout its flight; it does not float
distractorRationale.d: Gravity is fully present at launch; the thrust simply exceeds the weight

questions.stem: A ball of mass 0.15 kg strikes a wall horizontally at 20 m/s and rebounds along the same line at 15 m/s. The contact lasts 0.050 s. Calculate the average force exerted on the ball by the wall. Give your answer in newtons.
questions.explanation: Take the initial direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is $-15\ \text{m/s}$. Change in momentum $= m(v - u) = 0.15(-15 - 20) = 0.15 \times (-35) = -5.25\ \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Force $= \frac{\text{change in momentum}}{t} = \frac{5.25}{0.050} = 105\ \text{N}$, directed away from the wall. Forgetting the sign change on rebound would wrongly give $\frac{0.75}{0.05} = 15\ \text{N}$.

questions.stem: A body of mass 4.0 kg moving east at 6.0 m/s collides head-on with a body of mass 2.0 kg moving west at 3.0 m/s. The two stick together after impact. Calculate the magnitude of their common velocity. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: Take east as positive. Total momentum before $= (4.0)(+6.0) + (2.0)(-3.0) = 24 - 6 = 18\ \text{kg}\,\text{m}\,\text{s}^{-1}$. Total mass after $= 6.0\ \text{kg}$, so $v = \frac{18}{6.0} = 3.0\ \text{m/s}$. The positive sign shows the combined body moves east. Treating the westward velocity as positive would wrongly give 5 m/s.
